summary:
Visitors in Hauts-de-France stand under France's national framework: criminal law, identity-document rules, anti-discrimination law and marriage law apply uniformly across the region, and the country's oversight bodies record the same pattern of risk everywhere.

Prison placement is the region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk. Under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender inscribed on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities. Controller-general Adeline Hazan, the national detention inspector-general, identifies transgender detainees as the group that suffers the most in prison.

The BuzzFeed News investigation of 12 January 2018 documents that practice in the region directly. Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting "We don't want any women here!", was attacked with a knife by a fellow inmate and spent two days in solitary confinement. The same investigation records Kara B. held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial, and a Ministry of Justice count of 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 covering every place of deprivation of liberty and built from referrals received since 2010. It finds that assignment to establishments or wards is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and that searches of people whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
Prison placement is decided facility by facility rather than by statutory rule: each establishment improvises, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates, and accounts collected in the BuzzFeed News feature describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The CGLPL examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, together with ministry and association input, and recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform. The national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees; its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

Placement remained under parliamentary scrutiny in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in a men's prison outside the region and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in France rests on the justice-modernisation law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016; the CGLPL's 2021 opinion faults the prison administration for not translating that statute into prison rules, so residents held in custody continue to be assigned by civil status alone.

The Défenseur des droits' framework decision on trans rights sets out official guidance for service providers in France, drawn from case files and association testimony, and is the standing reference for residents challenging discrimination in accommodation and services.

Residents' anti-discrimination position is defined by persistent recorded discrimination rather than legal prohibition: the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey reports that 64% of trans people in France experience identity-related discrimination.

Partner recognition follows the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013, which legalised same-sex marriage nationally.
outOfScopeNotes:
No region-level data is sourced on border encounters, identity-document checks or prefectural ID-issuance practice within Hauts-de-France; the only region-specific detention account in the inventory is the Lille case from 2014, and the airport account dates from 2017 and does not identify a Hauts-de-France port of entry.

The current number of transgender detainees is not sourced. The only figure available is the Ministry of Justice count of 13 detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016, with no later national or regional count in the inventory.

Whether the 2016 justice-modernisation law has since been translated into prison rules is unresolved in the sources; the CGLPL's 2021 finding of non-translation is the most recent statement available.

No sourced material addresses trans-specific hate-crime offences, their charging or their enforcement in Hauts-de-France, nor access to gender-affirming healthcare in the region's facilities.
